fragments.text: Hello, thank you very much for the opportunity to participate in this conference. My name is Sizad Pita D'Souza and my presentation today is titled Data Silences, the practice of managing what we measure. My presentation today is structured as follows. I will firstly introduce the idea of data silences, talking through how I think it is constructed, what its key elements are, as well as a little bit in terms of what are the strategies that are employed to ensure that a data silence is engineered. I will thereafter talk about three specific case studies, one which looks at rule of law indices, the second which speaks about the migrant crisis during COVID-19 in India, and the

fragments.text: third is in relation to the ongoing genocide in Palestine. Thereafter I will briefly look at three strategies to combat data silences. So data silences are going to be our deliberate acts of commissions and omissions that are designed to tell a partial picture of the world that we live in. These actions are such that they are used to present information in a manner that places prominence on one form of knowledge over the other. There are instruments that are not only used to have a particular knowledge effect but they also have a governance effect because they privilege the ways in which particular decisions are made more often than not to support those who are in power. There are three strategies that I would like to put forward which explain this notion

fragments.text: of data silences. The first strategy is that data silences are created and engineered by commissioning certain constructions of worlds. They construct what information is important and necessary and in doing so create a reactivity around that information. The second aspect of a data silence is that of omitting experiences of worlds and in doing so limiting the possibility of bringing in valid concerns from a variety of other sources that would otherwise make situations more complex and more challenging. And the third strategy of a data silence is delegitimizing the experiences of people by questioning the very nature of how they created such data and as a consequence reducing the gravity of certain experiences particularly when they emerge from contexts and places

Rule of law indices are used to explain what the rule of law is. From these examples you can see the world justice project speaks of the rule of law in terms of constraints of government power, the absence of corruption, open government fundamental rights or insecurity, questions of regulatory enforcement, civil, criminal and formal justice. So having briefly outlined three different aspects of data silence, I'd like to end this presentation by firstly talking about the necessity of centering and ensuring that we engage with the political economy of data. By challenging who determines what data is valid or is invalid, secondly by problematizing this need for commensurability, so identifying a common vocabulary and asking the question that in creating a common vocabulary as we see it in rule of law indicators, what is it that is missing and whose voices are being silenced?
